docs.title: ENUMs Usage Reference — MT5Account
docs.text: Which low-level MT5Account methods take or return protobuf enums, and how you pass them in Ruby.

docs.title: 💎 How enums work in Ruby
docs.text:
In the Ruby protobuf runtime, an enum value is a Ruby symbol — both when you pass it in and when you read it back. There are no module constants to import (unlike Python/Node): you write the value's name as a :SYMBOL.

# IN — a property selector enum, passed as a symbol:
balance  = mt5.account.account_info_double(:ACCOUNT_BALANCE)      # AccountInfoDoublePropertyType
leverage = mt5.account.account_info_integer(:ACCOUNT_LEVERAGE)    # AccountInfoIntegerPropertyType
digits   = mt5.account.symbol_info_integer("EURUSD", :SYMBOL_DIGITS)

# OUT — an enum-typed field reads back as a symbol:
acc = mt5.account.account_summary
acc.account_trade_mode        # => :MRPC_ACCOUNT_TRADE_MODE_DEMO   (MrpcEnumAccountTradeMode)

Don't know a value's exact spelling? List any enum with the Protobuf Inspector:

ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb enum AccountInfoDoublePropertyType
ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb whereenum TMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE

Mind the context. Order-type lives in separate enums per call: TMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE (order_send), ENUM_ORDER_TYPE_TF (calculators / order_check), ENUM_ORDER_TYPE (margin rate), SUB_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE (streaming). See the table in Return Codes and Protobuf Inspector.

docs.title: ⚠️ Special cases
docs.text:
1. Result enums — SYMBOL_SECTOR / SYMBOL_INDUSTRY. Most selectors just pick a property, but two SymbolInfoIntegerProperty selectors return a value that is itself an enum code: symbol_info_integer(symbol, :SYMBOL_SECTOR) returns a BMT5_ENUM_SYMBOL_SECTOR value (14 of them) and :SYMBOL_INDUSTRY returns a BMT5_ENUM_SYMBOL_INDUSTRY value (152). The low-level call hands it back as a plain int64, so map the number yourself — ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb enum BMT5_ENUM_SYMBOL_INDUSTRY. The same values arrive already typed on SymbolParameters.sector / .industry from symbol_params_many.
  2. returned_code is not an enum. On trade results it's a plain uint32 (though its names live in the MqlErrorTradeCode enum). See Return Codes.

docs.title: Getting Started with RubyMT5
docs.text: Quick setup — connect to MetaTrader 5 from Ruby in a few minutes.

docs.title: What is RubyMT5?
docs.text:
RubyMT5 is a Ruby client for MetaTrader 5 accounts over the MetaRPC gRPC API (mt5.mrpc.pro:443). It's organised in three layers you can mix freely:

  • MT5Account — raw gRPC, protobuf in/out, full control.
  • MT5Service — typed Ruby Structs, plain arguments.
  • MT5Sugar — one-line helpers.

See the Project Map for how they fit together. (MetaRPC::MT5::Client aliases MT5Sugar.)

docs.title: Install & downloads
docs.text: Two ways to use RubyMT5 — take our ready-made project, or take only the protocol and build your own client.

docs.title: 1 · Take our project (recommended)
docs.text:
The complete thing we built: the three layers (MT5Sugar / MT5Service / MT5Account), the error/stream helpers, and the generated stubs — all wired together as the metarpc_mt5 gem.

  • Just the library, for your own app — the gem isn't on RubyGems, so point Bundler at the repo:
# Gemfile
gem "metarpc_mt5", git: "https://github.com/MetaRPC/RubyMT5.git"

bundle install

Then require "metarpc_mt5". Brings the SDK and the protobuf stubs (under the gem's package/).

  • The full repo (adds the runnable examples/demos/ and the tests):
git clone https://github.com/MetaRPC/RubyMT5.git
cd RubyMT5
bundle install
ruby examples/demos/main.rb 6     # run a demo (6 = sugar basics)

🎓 New here? Start with the full repo (the git clone above). You get all three layers side by side (MT5Account → MT5Service → MT5Sugar) and ready-made examples written on each of them that you can run and read. Learn the SDK this way first — only once you're comfortable should you consider building your own from the raw protos (option 2 below).

🪟 Windows note. The grpc gem ships prebuilt binaries for Windows (x64-mingw-ucrt) only through 1.84.1 — newer versions are source-only and need a full build toolchain. On Windows, pin it in your Gemfile: gem "grpc", "~> 1.84.1". (The repo's Gemfile already does this.)

docs.title: 2 · Take only the protos and build it yourself (raw gRPC)
docs.text:
For advanced use — after you know the SDK. Skip our layers and talk to the gateway from the generated stubs directly. The stubs ship in the package/ folder (mt5-term-api-*_pb.rb, *_services_pb.rb, and mrpc-mt5-error_pb.rb).

Download just the package/ folder (not the whole repo) — any of these:

# A) quickest — grab only the subfolder (no git history)
npx degit MetaRPC/RubyMT5/package package

# B) pure git — sparse-checkout only package/
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --no-checkout https://github.com/MetaRPC/RubyMT5.git
cd RubyMT5 && git sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'package/**' && git checkout

# C) via Bundler — then copy the folder out of the installed gem
bundle install          # with the Gemfile git source above
cp -r "$(bundle show metarpc_mt5)/package" ./package

Then install the gRPC + protobuf runtime next to it:

gem install grpc -v 1.84.1 google-protobuf googleapis-common-protos-types

Put package/ on the load path and require the service stubs:

$LOAD_PATH.unshift(File.expand_path("package", __dir__))
require "mt5-term-api-market-info_services_pb"   # etc.

The raw .proto sources (to regenerate stubs for another language or version) are on the MT5 Client API Explorer → Download MT5 Protos.

⚠️ The stubs are not standalone — take the whole package/ folder, not single files. Each *_pb.rb cross-requires its siblings (e.g. mrpc-mt5-error_pb) by bare name, so package/ must be on $LOAD_PATH. This path gives you raw gRPC with no 3-layer SDK — see the Protobuf Inspector.

docs.title: 🔑 API Key & Authentication
docs.text:
Connecting to the MetaRPC production endpoint (mt5.mrpc.pro:443) uses a personal API key — you get one just by registering on our site:

  1. Sign up — create a free account at https://mrpc.pro/signup.
  2. Copy your key — it's provisioned automatically; open the MT5 Client API Explorer and your key is shown at the top (Active · Copy key). Nothing to generate.
  3. Use it — pass the key to MT5Sugar.create(host, port, api_key:) (or set the MRPC_API_KEY environment variable instead of hard-coding it).

You'll also need an MT5 demo account (login / password / server, e.g. MetaQuotes-Demo) — see MT5 for Beginners to create one (one click for $1, or free via the MT5 terminal).

💡 TRIAL / keyless. No account yet? Pass the literal value "TRIAL" as the key to connect for a first look. Your own key — free from sign-up — is for normal use.

docs.title: 🆔 Session ID is automatic
docs.text: You never call get_id or supply an id header. On connect / connect_ex the server generates a terminal session GUID (terminal_instance_guid) and the SDK attaches it — alongside your API key — to every later request and stream automatically. Prefer passing a stable id: per strategy so the gateway reuses one terminal.

docs.title: Connect & read the account
docs.text:
require "metarpc_mt5"

mt5 = MetaRPC::MT5::MT5Sugar.create("mt5.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])
mt5.connect(5057947437, "password", server: "MetaQuotes-Demo")

a = mt5.account_info
puts "##{a.login} — #{a.balance} #{a.currency} · 1:#{a.leverage}"

Prefer environment variables? Set MT5_LOGIN / MT5_PASSWORD / MT5_SERVER and read them into mt5.quick_connect(login, password, server).

docs.title: A first trade (demo)
docs.text:
r = mt5.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)          # tiny demo position
puts r.returned_code == 10_009 ? "opened ##{r.order}" : r.returned_code_description

pos = mt5.open_positions(symbol: "EURUSD").max_by(&:ticket)
mt5.close_position(pos.ticket) if pos

Trading one-liners return the result *Data — check returned_code (10009 = DONE). A hard failure raises MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError (and a transport failure after the request may have reached the terminal raises a TradeOutcomeUnknown-marked error — don't blindly retry). See Return Codes & the error model.

docs.title: Dropping down a layer
docs.text:
Need something the sugar layer doesn't expose? Go down:

service = mt5.service   # MT5Service — typed Structs
account = mt5.account   # MT5Account — raw protobuf

q    = service.quote("EURUSD")             # Quote(bid, ask, spread, …)
tick = account.symbol_info_tick("EURUSD")  # raw MrpcMqlTick

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: The MT5, trading and SDK terms you'll meet in these docs, grouped by kind.

docs.title: 🏗️ Architectural terms
docs.text:
Three-layer architecture — the SDK is three decoupled layers, each owning the one below (sugar.service → MT5Service, service.account → MT5Account). See the Project Map.

MT5Account — the low-level layer. Raw gRPC: you pass protobuf *Request messages and read *Reply / *Data replies via their snake_case accessors. Owns the channel, the gRPC stubs, auth metadata, reconnect and streaming. → overview

MT5Service — the mid layer. Same calls, but it builds the protobuf from plain arguments and returns typed Ruby Structs (Account, Quote…). → overview

MT5Sugar — the high layer. One-line helpers (buy_market, close_all_positions) with smart defaults; trade helpers return the result data (check returned_code). → overview

Struct (DTO) — the plain Ruby Struct objects MT5Service returns instead of protobuf (Account, Quote…), with read-only attribute methods.

ApiError — the error raised when the gateway or terminal reports a problem (MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError). InvalidLoginError flags never-retry auth failures; TradeOutcomeUnknown marks a trade whose result is uncertain after a transport failure. See Return Codes → the error model.

Subscription — what a streaming method returns (MetaRPC::MT5::Subscription): call cancel to stop the stream; count / error report its state.

Client / Account aliases — MetaRPC::MT5::Client aliases MT5Sugar; MetaRPC::MT5::Account aliases MT5Account.

docs.title: 💎 Ruby-specific concepts
docs.text:
Blocks for streams — a streaming method yields each payload to the block you pass, and returns a Subscription to stop it.

sub = mt5.on_symbol_tick("EURUSD") { |t| puts "#{t.bid} / #{t.ask}" }
# later:
sub.cancel

Keyword arguments — optional parameters are passed by name, not position.

mt5.connect(5057947437, "password", server: "MetaQuotes-Demo")
mt5.buy_market_with_sl_tp("EURUSD", 0.01, sl: 1.0820, tp: 1.0920, comment: "demo")

Enums as symbols — protobuf enums are Ruby symbols, both in and out (:MRPC_ACCOUNT_TRADE_MODE_DEMO, :ACCOUNT_BALANCE). See the ENUMs Reference.

mode = mt5.account.account_info_double(:ACCOUNT_BALANCE)

Typed Structs vs protobuf stubs — the low layer returns generated protobuf objects (snake_case accessors like reply.account_balance); the mid layer unwraps them into typed Structs. Discover real field names with the Protobuf Inspector.

d = mt5.account.opened_orders          # low: protobuf, d.position_infos
ps = mt5.service.opened_orders         # mid: typed objects

Error handling — begin / rescue — wrap calls that can fail; rescue MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError (or its subclasses).

begin
  mt5.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)
rescue MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError => e
  warn "trade failed: #{e.message}"
end

Connection & cleanup — connect / quick_connect opens the terminal session; disconnect closes it and frees the terminal (a trial allows one per IP). Use ensure.

begin
  # …
ensure
  mt5.disconnect
end

docs.title: Account
docs.text: Balance — closed-trade money; excludes floating P/L. Equity — balance + floating P/L; moves with open positions. Margin — funds locked to hold positions. Free margin — equity − margin; available to open more. Margin level — equity / margin × 100 (%); low levels risk a stop-out. Leverage — the multiplier (1:100) setting margin need. Trade mode — DEMO, CONTEST or REAL.

docs.title: Instruments & prices
docs.text: Symbol — a tradable instrument (EURUSD, XAUUSD). Bid / Ask — sell / buy price; spread = ask − bid. Digits — decimal places (5 for EURUSD, 3 for JPY). Tick — one price update (symbol_info_tick / on_symbol_tick). DOM (Depth of Market) — the order book: pending volume at each price level.

docs.title: Orders, positions & deals (MT5 model)
docs.text: Order — an instruction to trade. Market fills now; pending (LIMIT/STOP/STOP_LIMIT) waits for a price. Position — an open trade; on MT5 distinct from the order and the deals. Deal — a single execution (fill); a position is the net of its deals. Ticket — the numeric id (a filled market order's order ticket = its position ticket). Order type — three different enums by context: TMT5_ORDER_TYPE_* (order_send), ORDER_TYPE_TF_* (calculators / order_check), MQL ORDER_TYPE_* (margin rate). BUY=0, SELL=1, …. Position type: 0 = BUY, 1 = SELL. SL / TP — stop-loss / take-profit auto-close levels. Magic number — a client id tagging a strategy's orders. RetCode (returned_code) — the trade-server return code; 10009 = DONE. See Return Codes.

docs.title: 📦 Technical concepts
docs.text:
Point — the smallest price increment (0.00001 on 5-digit EURUSD). Pip — the conventional move unit; on a 3- or 5-digit symbol pip = point × 10, so one pip on EURUSD = 0.0001. Tick value / tick size — the money value of one tick, and the price change one tick represents — inputs for P&L and sizing.

Lot / volume — trade size in lots (0.01 = micro). Must obey volume limits (volume_min / volume_max / volume_step). Contract size — units of the base instrument per 1.0 lot.

Risk-based sizing — picking the lot so a stop of N pips loses a fixed amount: combine calc_profit, required_margin and max_lot. Risk amount = balance × risk_percent / 100. Required margin — margin a prospective order needs. Drawdown — the drop from a peak to current equity, %.

Stops level (SYMBOL_TRADE_STOPS_LEVEL) — minimum distance, in points, SL/TP may sit from the market; closer → retcode 10016.

Trailing stop — a stop that ratchets in your favour, never back (orchestrator). Breakeven — moving the stop to entry once in profit. Hedging — holding BUY and SELL on one symbol at once (hedging accounts). Grid trading — bracketing price with pending orders (orchestrator). Scalping — many small short-lived trades. News trading — trading around releases; expect wide spreads / rejections. Kill-switch — close everything on a drawdown/margin breach (risk manager).

docs.title: 🔌 gRPC & protocol terms
docs.text:
gRPC — the RPC protocol the SDK speaks to mt5.mrpc.pro:443 (HTTP/2 + protobuf over TLS).

Protobuf — the binary message format. On the low layer you build *Request messages and read *Reply replies via snake_case accessors; MT5Service hides this behind typed Structs. The generated stubs live in package/.

Streaming pattern — a server stream delivered via a block: a streaming method yields each payload and returns a Subscription. See gRPC Stream Management.

Gateway — the MetaRPC service (mt5.mrpc.pro) bridging the SDK to MT5 terminals and managing sessions. Terminal — the MT5 instance your account runs on behind the gateway. Session / terminal instance guid — the id obtained on connect (ConnectEx), attached with your API key to every later call automatically (on mt5.account.server_guid). API key — your MetaRPC key; pass it to MT5Sugar.create(...), or use "TRIAL".

docs.title: gRPC Streaming & Subscription Management
docs.text:
How real-time server streams work in RubyMT5 — subscribe with a block, stop cleanly with cancel, and never leak a reader thread.

This guide covers:

  • ✅ How to subscribe to market-data and trade-event streams
  • ✅ How to stop a stream without leaking its background thread
  • ✅ Patterns from a 5-second snapshot to a managed background service
  • ✅ The model behind every stream (one thread + a Subscription)
  • ✅ Error handling and best practices

docs.title: The model in one picture
docs.text:
Every streaming method takes a block and immediately returns a MetaRPC::MT5::Subscription. The actual reading happens on a background thread the SDK spawns for you — your block is called once per message as it arrives, while your main code keeps running.

your block  ◄──yields each message──  background Thread  ◄──gRPC server stream──  mt5.mrpc.pro:443
     ▲                                        │
     └──────────  sub.cancel  stops the thread (and joins it, up to 5 s)

There is no polling and no async/await — Ruby threads do the work. A Subscription is the handle you keep to stop it (cancel), wait on it (join), check it (alive?, count, error). This is the whole lifecycle; master cancel and you're done.

docs.title: Quick Start — the simplest subscription
docs.text:
require "metarpc_mt5"

mt5 = MetaRPC::MT5::MT5Sugar.create("mt5.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])
mt5.quick_connect(5057947437, "password", "MetaQuotes-Demo")

# on_symbol_tick / subscribe_ticks yields each tick to the block, returns a Subscription
sub = mt5.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") do |t|
  puts "#{t.symbol}  bid #{t.bid}  ask #{t.ask}"
end

sleep 5        # let it stream for 5 seconds while the main thread does other work
sub.cancel     # stop cleanly — cancels the stream and joins the reader thread
puts "received #{sub.count} ticks"

When to use: quick examples, testing, short monitoring sessions.

subscribe_ticks (sugar/service) and on_symbol_tick (account) are the same stream — the sugar name just reads better. The block receives a tick (symbol, bid, ask, last, volume, time, flags), not a wrapper.

docs.title: Available streaming methods
docs.text:
All of these take a block and return a Subscription. They exist on MT5Account (raw) and are re-exposed by MT5Service / MT5Sugar under friendlier names.

Method (Account) Sugar / Service name Yields What it streams on_symbol_tick(symbols) subscribe_ticks(symbols) a tick real-time bid/ask per symbol on_trade on_trade OnTradeData orders/positions changed on_position_profit(interval_ms:, ignore_empty:) on_position_profit(...) OnPositionProfitData position P/L, every interval_ms on_positions_and_pending_orders_tickets(interval_ms:) on_tickets(interval_ms:) tickets snapshot open position & pending-order tickets on_trade_transaction on_trade_transaction OnTradeTransactionData low-level MT5 trade transactions

Plus a blocking convenience that streams ticks for a fixed time and returns the count (no Subscription to manage):

n = mt5.each_tick("EURUSD", seconds: 5) { |t| puts t.bid }   # blocks 5 s, then returns n

Reference: Streaming Methods overview · MT5Sugar → Streaming. Run it: ruby examples/demos/main.rb 3 (raw) · ruby examples/demos/main.rb 5 (service).

docs.title: Pattern 1 — Time-boxed snapshot
docs.text:
The blocking each_tick is the shortest path when you just want N seconds of data:

count = mt5.each_tick(["EURUSD", "GBPUSD"], seconds: 10) do |t|
  puts "#{t.symbol}: #{t.bid}"
end
puts "#{count} ticks in 10s"

docs.title: Pattern 2 — Count-limited (stop after N messages)
docs.text:
Keep the Subscription and cancel it from inside the block once you've seen enough:

sub = nil
seen = 0
sub = mt5.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") do |t|
  seen += 1
  puts "[#{seen}] #{t.bid}"
  Thread.new { sub.cancel } if seen >= 50   # cancel off the reader thread
end
sub.join        # wait for it to finish

Why Thread.new { sub.cancel }? cancel joins the reader thread, so calling it from that same thread would deadlock. Cancel from the main thread (Pattern 3) or hand it off to a short-lived thread as above.

docs.title: Pattern 3 — Condition-based stop (from the main thread)
docs.text:
Signal with a flag; the main thread does the cancel:

target_hit = false
sub = mt5.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") { |t| target_hit = true if t.bid > 1.10000 }

sleep 0.1 until target_hit || !sub.alive?
sub.cancel
puts target_hit ? "target reached after #{sub.count} ticks" : "stream ended early"

docs.title: Pattern 4 — Background service with guaranteed cleanup
docs.text:
Wrap the lifetime in begin/ensure so the stream is always stopped, even on error or Ctrl-C:

sub = mt5.on_position_profit(interval_ms: 1000) do |data|
  data.updated_positions.sort_by { |p| -p.profit }.first(5).each do |p|
    puts "#{p.position_symbol}  #{p.profit.round(2)}"
  end
end

begin
  sleep 30            # run the service for 30 s (or loop your own logic here)
ensure
  sub.cancel          # ALWAYS stop it
end

docs.title: Multiple concurrent streams
docs.text:
Each subscription is independent (its own thread), so just open several and cancel them all. Collect the handles so cleanup is one loop:

subs = []
subs << mt5.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") { |t| puts "[TICK] #{t.bid}" }
subs << mt5.on_trade              { |_e| puts "[TRADE] event" }
subs << mt5.on_position_profit(interval_ms: 2000) { |d| puts "[P/L] #{d.updated_positions.size} positions" }

begin
  sleep 30
ensure
  subs.each(&:cancel)   # stop every stream
end

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
A stream's reader thread swallows the expected GRPC::Cancelled on cancel. Any other error is stored on the subscription as sub.error (it does not raise in your main thread), and the thread ends — so a stream can stop on its own:

sub = mt5.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") { |t| handle(t) }
sleep 10
sub.cancel

if sub.error
  warn "stream failed: #{sub.error.class}: #{sub.error.message}"   # e.g. a MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError
end

Check sub.alive? to see whether a stream is still running, and sub.count for how many messages it has delivered. A per-message error reported by the server (a *Reply with an error) is raised inside the thread as MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError and lands in sub.error. See Return Codes & the error model.

docs.title: ✅ DO
docs.text:
1. Always keep the Subscription a streaming method returns — it's your only handle to stop it.
  2. Always cancel when done (wrap long-lived streams in begin/ensure).
  3. Cancel from the main thread (or a throwaway thread), never from inside the reader block — cancel joins the thread.
  4. Prefer each_tick for simple time-boxed sampling — it manages the subscription for you.
  5. Check sub.error after a stream you expected to keep running has stopped.
  6. Collect handles (subs << …) when running several streams, so cleanup is one each(&:cancel).

docs.title: ❌ DON'T
docs.text:
1. Don't drop the handle (mt5.subscribe_ticks(...) { } with no sub =) — you can never stop that thread.
  2. Don't call sub.cancel inside its own block — it deadlocks (join-on-self). Signal a flag or spawn a thread.
  3. Don't forget ensure — an exception in your loop would otherwise leave the reader thread running.
  4. Don't assume a stream is alive — the server or network can end it; re-check alive? / error.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Streaming Methods overview — every stream, with its payload fields
  • OnSymbolTick · OnTrade — per-method references
  • MT5Sugar → Streaming — the friendly subscribe_ticks / each_tick helpers
  • Glossary → Subscription · Return Codes & errors

Remember: one block, one background thread, one Subscription. Keep the handle, cancel in an ensure, and your streaming code stays leak-free. 🚀

docs.title: MT5 for Beginners
docs.text: New to MetaTrader 5? This is the 5-minute mental model you need before the code makes sense.

docs.title: What MT5 is
docs.text:
MetaTrader 5 (MT5) is a trading platform. Your account lives on a broker's server (e.g. MetaQuotes-Demo). Through it you trade symbols (instruments like EURUSD or XAUUSD).

This SDK talks to your MT5 terminal over the network (gRPC to mt5.mrpc.pro:443) so you can automate everything from Ruby.

Always learn on a demo account. It trades with fake money on real prices — no risk.

docs.title: Getting a demo account & API key
docs.text:
Registration and your API key are free. Sign up at mrpc.pro/signup and your key is provisioned automatically — nothing to generate; in the web Explorer it's even attached to every call for you. What costs money is paid usage of the service (for example the instant $1 demo below).

To run the SDK you also need an MT5 demo account (login / password / server). You can get one two ways:

docs.title: ⚡ Fastest — one click on mrpc.pro ($1)
docs.text:
Our MT5 Client API Explorer (a live API playground) spins up a demo account instantly — no terminal install:

  1. Open the MT5 Client API Explorer (sign in first). Your API key is already shown at the top (Active · Copy key).
  2. The demo server is fixed to MetaQuotes-Demo. Click Open demo account ($1). The $1 is charged to your MetaRPC balance (the account that holds your API key) — not to a broker.
  3. The demo is created instantly with a ready login / password / server — you can even run real API calls right on that page (the key is attached automatically).

Copy the demo login / password / server, then jump to Getting Started to connect from Ruby.

docs.title: 🖥️ Free — create a demo in the MetaTrader 5 terminal
docs.text:
The no-cost route: create a MetaQuotes demo account directly in the MT5 terminal (free), and connect with your free API key — or with the literal value "TRIAL" for a quick first look.

1 · Download & install MT5. Get the terminal from metatrader5.com/download and install it.

2 · Find the Navigator panel. It's on the left, below Market Watch. Its Accounts section is where you add accounts.

3 · Open a new account. Right-click Accounts → Open an account to bring up the broker-server search.

4 · Pick the MetaQuotes demo server. Find MetaQuotes-Demo (search if needed) and click Next.

5 · Choose "Open a new demo account" and click Next.

6 · Fill in the form (name, email; virtual deposit e.g. $10,000, leverage 1:100, currency USD), accept the terms, Next.

7 · Save your credentials. MT5 shows your login, password (master) and server (MetaQuotes-Demo). Copy them now — the SDK needs exactly these three values.

Two passwords are shown: the master password trades; the investor password is read-only. Use the master password with the SDK.

docs.title: The money words
docs.text:
Term In one line Balance Your settled money (no open trades counted). Equity Balance plus the profit/loss of trades you have open right now. Margin Money "reserved" while a trade is open. Free margin What's left to open new trades.

When you open a trade, equity moves tick by tick. When you close it, the result folds into balance.

docs.title: Buying and selling
docs.text:
• Buy (go long) — you profit if the price rises.
  • Sell (go short) — you profit if the price falls.

You trade in lots (volume). 0.01 is a micro lot — the smallest typical size, perfect for learning.

Two ways to enter:

  • Market order — fill now at the current price.
  • Pending order — wait for a price. A LIMIT waits for a better price; a STOP waits for a breakout.

docs.title: Protecting a trade
docs.text:
• Stop-Loss (SL) — auto-close if the price goes against you by so much. Caps the loss.
  • Take-Profit (TP) — auto-close once you've made your target.

Set them as prices — compute the distances from pips (pip = point × 10 on a 5-digit symbol):

pip    = mt5.symbol_point("EURUSD") * 10
digits = mt5.symbol_digits("EURUSD")
q      = mt5.price("EURUSD")

# 20-pip stop, 40-pip target
mt5.buy_market_with_sl_tp("EURUSD", 0.01,
  sl: (q.bid - 20 * pip).round(digits),
  tp: (q.ask + 40 * pip).round(digits))

See Risk Management for sizing a trade to a fixed risk.

docs.title: MT5's model: orders, positions, deals
docs.text:
This trips up newcomers, so remember:

  • An order is the instruction.
  • A position is the resulting open trade.
  • A deal is each execution (fill) that builds a position.

On MT5 these are separate things (unlike MT4). A filled market BUY gives you a position, identified by a ticket.

docs.title: Your first 10 lines
docs.text:
require "metarpc_mt5"

mt5 = MetaRPC::MT5::MT5Sugar.create("mt5.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])
mt5.quick_connect(login, "password", "MetaQuotes-Demo")

puts "balance #{mt5.balance.round(2)}"
r = mt5.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)          # tiny demo trade
mt5.close_position(r.order)                  # r.order is the position ticket

docs.title: 🧱 The three layers
docs.text:
RubyMT5 is built in three decoupled layers. Your code can enter at any level, and each layer owns the one beneath it (sugar.service → the MT5Service, service.account → the MT5Account). MetaRPC::MT5::Client aliases MT5Sugar; Account aliases MT5Account.

Layer Source What it does Overview 3 · MT5Sugar lib/metarpc_mt5/mt5_sugar.rb One-line helpers: buy_market, close_all_positions, risk sizing, SL/TP. 13 groups. MT5Sugar overview 2 · MT5Service lib/metarpc_mt5/mt5_service.rb Typed facade: plain args in, typed Ruby Structs out (Account, Quote). No protobuf. 6 groups. MT5Service overview 1 · MT5Account lib/metarpc_mt5/mt5_account.rb Low-level gRPC: protobuf request/reply, connect/session, reconnect, streaming. Everything builds on it. 7 groups. MT5Account overview 
Your code  →  MT5Sugar  →  MT5Service  →  MT5Account  →  gRPC  →  mt5.mrpc.pro:443  →  MT5 terminal

docs.title: 🎮 Running the demos
docs.text:
The demos (laid out in the tree above) run from one menu — pass a number to run one directly:

ruby examples/demos/main.rb          # interactive menu
ruby examples/demos/main.rb 6        # sugar basics
ruby examples/demos/main.rb 11       # trailing-stop orchestrator

Config comes from examples/demos/config/config.json or the env vars MT5_LOGIN / MT5_PASSWORD / MT5_SERVER / MT5_SYMBOL / MT5_VOLUME / MRPC_API_KEY.

docs.title: 🎯 Which layer should you use?
docs.text:
• Most trading apps → MT5Sugar. One-liners, risk-based sizing and SL/TP keep your code short and safe.
  • Custom execution → MT5Service. Typed calls when you manage your own flow.
  • Protocol-level control → MT5Account. Raw protobuf requests and streams.
  • New to MT5? → MT5 for Beginners, then Getting Started.
  • Mirror trades to other accounts? → SDK Ecosystem → Trade Copier.

docs.title: Protobuf Inspector — Interactive Type Explorer
docs.text:
A small offline tool that reads the generated MT5 protobuf stubs and tells you the real field names, types and enum values — so you never guess an accessor again.

The generated stubs under package/*_pb.rb are the raw contract. When you need to know "what's the exact accessor on this reply?" or "what are the valid values of this enum?", the inspector answers from the descriptors themselves — no connection, no API key, no trades.

Source: examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb

docs.title: 🏁 Running it
docs.text:
It's a standalone helper (it does not go through the demo menu, which connects first):

# interactive REPL
ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb

# one-shot — pass a command as arguments, get the answer, exit
ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb OnSymbolTickRequest
ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb enum TMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE
ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb field position_ticket
ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb search Tick

The REPL opens on a summary of what it discovered:

================================================================
MT5 PROTOBUF INSPECTOR (Ruby)
================================================================
  321 message types · 74 enums discovered
  Type 'help' for commands, 'list' to browse, 'exit' to quit.

>

Offline & safe. It only requires the package/*_pb.rb message stubs and reads their descriptors. It never opens a channel. You can run it with no credentials at all.

docs.title: 🧰 Commands
docs.text:
Command What it shows Example list [--msg\|--enum] all message types and/or enums list --enum <TypeName> a message's fields (name · type · label · #) PositionHistoryInfo search <text> message and enum names containing <text> search Order field <name> which messages carry a field named <name> field position_ticket findtype <type> every field of a proto type, grouped by message findtype double enum <Name> an enum's values (sorted by number) enum TMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE whereenum <Name> which message fields use an enum whereenum BMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE stats type / field / enum counts stats help or ? the command list help exit / quit / q leave the REPL exit

Name lookups are fuzzy: exact → case-insensitive exact → a single partial match → otherwise it lists the candidates.

docs.title: A message's fields — <TypeName>
docs.text:
Fields print as name · proto-type · label · field-number. Message/enum fields show their subtype inline (enum<…> / message<…>):

> OnTradeData

TYPE: OnTradeData   (4 fields)
================================================================
  type                       enum<MT5_SUB_ENUM_EVENT_GROUP_TYPE>           (#1)
  event_data                 message<OnTadeEventData>           (#2)
  account_info               message<OnEventAccountInfo>           (#3)
  terminal_instance_guid_id  string                           (#4)

The field name is the accessor you call in Ruby (data.event_data, data.account_info). This is how you catch the naming gotchas the stubs hide — for example TickSizeSymbol uses PascalCase accessors:

> TickSizeSymbol

TYPE: TickSizeSymbol   (7 fields)
================================================================
  Index                 int32                            (#1)
  Name                  string                           (#2)
  TradeTickValue        double                           (#3)   ← t.TradeTickValue, not t.trade_tick_value
  TradeTickValueProfit  double                           (#4)
  TradeTickValueLoss    double                           (#5)
  TradeTickSize         double                           (#6)
  TradeContractSize     double                           (#7)

docs.title: Which message has a field? — field <name>
docs.text:
> field position_ticket

FIELD 'position_ticket'
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
exact match in (3): MqlTradeRequest, MqlTradeTransaction, PositionHistoryInfo

partial (2): OnPositionsAndPendingOrdersTicketsData (position_tickets), OpenedOrdersTicketsData (opened_position_tickets)

So on a position-history row the accessor is position_ticket, not ticket — the kind of mistake this command ends in seconds.

docs.title: An enum's values — enum <Name>
docs.text:
> enum TMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE

ENUM: TMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE
================================================================
  TMT5_ORDER_TYPE_BUY             = 0
  TMT5_ORDER_TYPE_SELL            = 1
  TMT5_ORDER_TYPE_BUY_LIMIT       = 2
  TMT5_ORDER_TYPE_SELL_LIMIT      = 3
  TMT5_ORDER_TYPE_BUY_STOP        = 4
  TMT5_ORDER_TYPE_SELL_STOP       = 5
  TMT5_ORDER_TYPE_BUY_STOP_LIMIT  = 6
  TMT5_ORDER_TYPE_SELL_STOP_LIMIT = 7
  TMT5_ORDER_TYPE_CLOSE_BY        = 8

docs.title: Where is an enum used? — whereenum <Name>
docs.text:
> whereenum BMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE

ENUM 'BMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE' used in (4 fields)
================================================================
  HistoryOrderInfo.type
  OpenedOrderInfo.type
  OrderHistoryData.type
  SymbolParameters.order_mode

docs.title: All fields of a type — findtype <type>
docs.text:
> findtype double

FIELDS OF TYPE 'double' (292 in 56 messages)
================================================================
  AccountInfoDoubleData: requested_value
  AccountSummaryData: account_balance, account_equity, account_credit, account_margin, account_margin_free, account_margin_level
  …

Valid type names are the proto scalar/compound types: double, float, string, bool, int32, int64, uint32, uint64, message, enum.

docs.title: 🧭 The "three order_type enums" gotcha
docs.text:
search order_type reveals why a BUY constant that works in one call fails in another — the API has separate order-type enums per context:

> search order_type
enums (13): … BMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE, ENUM_ORDER_TYPE, ENUM_ORDER_TYPE_TF,
            SUB_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE, TMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE, …
Enum Use it for TMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE order_send (opening/placing orders) ENUM_ORDER_TYPE_TF calculators / order_check (order_calc_margin, order_calc_profit) ENUM_ORDER_TYPE (MQL) symbol_info_margin_rate SUB_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE streaming events (on_trade, on_trade_transaction)

When a call rejects your enum, whereenum <Name> confirms whether that enum is even accepted by the message you're building. See ENUMs Reference for the full picture.

docs.title: 📦 Common use cases
docs.text:
1. "undefined method on a reply." Run <ReplyType> and read the real field names — e.g. a history row exposes position_ticket, not ticket.
  2. "What value do I pass for order_type?" enum TMT5_ENUM_ORDER_TYPE (and mind the context table above).
  3. "Which request/reply do I need?" search <keyword> lists both messages and enums matching the name.
  4. "Which messages even have this field?" field <name> — exact and partial hits with the real field spelling.
  5. "Where is this enum accepted?" whereenum <Name> before you build the request.

docs.title: ℹ️ How it works
docs.text:
Ruby's protobuf runtime exposes a descriptor on every generated type. The inspector walks the Mt5TermApi namespace, classifies each constant as a message (Google::Protobuf::Descriptor) or an enum (Google::Protobuf::EnumDescriptor), and reads fields (name, type, label, number, subtype) and enum pairs straight from those descriptors. That's why it's always in sync with the stubs — there's no hand-maintained list to drift.

Because Ruby descriptors carry field numbers, proto types, labels and subtypes, this inspector reports more than the raw getter/setter names you'd see in some other SDKs — you get the full field shape.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• MT5Account overview — the documented API over these stubs
  • ENUMs Reference — which enum belongs to which call
  • Return Codes & errors — returned_code and the error model
  • Getting Started → raw gRPC — taking only the package/ stubs

Tip: reach for the inspector the moment a field or enum name is in doubt — one field or enum lookup is faster than reading a stub by hand.

docs.title: Return Codes & the Error Model
docs.text: How RubyMT5 tells you a trade's result: returned_code on the data it returns, ApiError when the call itself fails, and TradeOutcomeUnknown when a trade's fate is uncertain.

docs.title: 🛡️ What returned_code is
docs.text:
RetCode (returned_code) is the trade-server status returned after a trading operation. 10009 = done. Anything else is the reason the broker rejected or deferred the trade (not enough money, market closed, bad stops…).

RetCodes appear only on trading operations, because only those go through the broker and can be rejected. Read-only calls (prices, symbols, balance) have no RetCode — they either return data or raise.

r = mt5.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)       # returns OrderSendData — it does NOT raise on a rejection
if r.returned_code == 10_009             # TRADE_RETCODE_DONE
  puts "opened ##{r.order}"
else
  puts "rejected: #{r.returned_code} #{r.returned_code_description}"
end

Golden rule: no exception ≠ trade succeeded. The call returning without raising only means the request reached the terminal. Always check returned_code.

docs.title: 🧭 The three outcomes of a trade call
docs.text:
Outcome How it surfaces What it means Done returned data, returned_code == 10009 the broker executed it Rejected / deferred returned data, returned_code != 10009 broker said no (or requote) — reason in returned_code_description Call failed raises MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError gateway/terminal error branch (validation, timeout, bad API key…) Uncertain raises …::ApiError or a TradeOutcomeUnknown-marked error request may or may not have executed — do not blindly retry

So a complete trade looks like:

begin
  r = mt5.buy_market_with_sl_tp("EURUSD", 0.01, sl: 1.0820, tp: 1.0920)
  if r.returned_code == 10_009
    puts "opened ##{r.order} @ #{r.price}"
  else
    puts "rejected: #{r.returned_string_code} — #{r.returned_code_description}"
  end
rescue MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError => e
  raise if e.trade_outcome_unknown?           # uncertain — check positions before retrying
  warn "trade error: #{e.error.mql_error_trade_description}"
end

docs.title: 📥 What the trade data carries
docs.text:
Trade one-liners return the operation's *Data (OrderSendData, OrderModifyData, OrderCloseData). The send result's fields:

> OrderSendData              # ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb OrderSendData
  returned_code              uint32    ← 10009 = DONE
  deal                       uint64
  order                      uint64    ← the position/order ticket on success
  volume                     double
  price                      double
  returned_string_code       string    ← e.g. "TRADE_RETCODE_NO_MONEY"
  returned_code_description  string    ← human text, straight from the server
  …

You rarely need a lookup table: every result already carries returned_string_code (the symbolic name) and returned_code_description (human text). The symbolic names are the protobuf enum MqlErrorTradeCode — list them all with the inspector:

ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb enum MqlErrorTradeCode

docs.title: ❗ The error object (MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError)
docs.text:
When the gateway answers with the error branch, the SDK raises MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError, wrapping the protobuf Error. Useful accessors:

On the error Gives e.message the full formatted string (code, type, MQL + trade codes, descriptions) e.code the gateway error_code string (e.g. "MRPC_TIMEOUT", "API_KEY_INVALID") e.error.mql_error_trade_int_code the numeric trade retcode (e.g. 10019) e.error.mql_error_trade_code the retcode as an enum symbol (e.g. :TRADE_RETCODE_NO_MONEY) e.error.mql_error_trade_description human trade-error text e.api_key_error? true for API_KEY_INVALID / API_KEY_REQUIRED — never retry e.trade_outcome_unknown? true when the trade's result is uncertain (see below)

Subclass InvalidLoginError < ApiError is raised by connect when the broker rejects the login — never retry it.

rescue MetaRPC::MT5::InvalidLoginError
  abort "bad login/password/server"
rescue MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError => e
  case e.error.mql_error_trade_int_code
  when 10_019 then warn "not enough money — reduce volume"
  when 10_018 then warn "market closed — try during trading hours"
  when 10_016 then warn "stops too close — widen SL/TP (StopLevel)"
  else warn "error #{e.code}: #{e.error.mql_error_trade_description}"
  end
end

docs.title: ⚠️ TradeOutcomeUnknown — the one you must not retry blindly
docs.text:
A trade call can fail after the request may already have reached the terminal (a gateway/terminal timeout, or a transport drop like gRPC UNAVAILABLE / DEADLINE_EXCEEDED). The trade may or may not have executed. The SDK never re-sends a trade automatically.

Two ways it reaches you, both answering trade_outcome_unknown? == true:

begin
  r = mt5.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)
rescue MetaRPC::MT5::TradeOutcomeUnknown => e   # transport failure, mixed into the GRPC error
  warn e.to_s
  # check whether it actually opened before doing anything:
  pos = mt5.open_positions(symbol: "EURUSD").max_by(&:ticket)
  # decide to keep it or send again — never retry unconditionally
rescue MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError => e
  retry_safely unless e.trade_outcome_unknown?  # in-band timeout (10012/10028/10031, MRPC_TIMEOUT…)
end

In-band uncertainty is flagged for trade RPCs when the code is a timeout (MRPC_TIMEOUT, TERMINAL_API_TIMEOUT, …) or the trade retcode is 10012 (TIMEOUT), 10028 (LOCKED) or 10031 (CONNECTION).

docs.title: 📋 Complete RetCode list (MqlErrorTradeCode)
docs.text: These are the standard MQL5 trade return codes, exactly as the enum defines them in package/. Bold = success.

docs.title: Success & partial
docs.text: Code Name Meaning 10009 TRADE_RETCODE_DONE request completed — the one you check for 10008 TRADE_RETCODE_PLACED pending order placed 10010 TRADE_RETCODE_DONE_PARTIAL only part of the volume filled

docs.title: Requote — retry with a fresh price
docs.text: Code Name 10004 TRADE_RETCODE_REQUOTE 10020 TRADE_RETCODE_PRICE_CHANGED

docs.title: Temporary — retry with a delay
docs.text: Code Name 10012 TRADE_RETCODE_TIMEOUT 10021 TRADE_RETCODE_PRICE_OFF (no quotes) 10024 TRADE_RETCODE_TOO_MANY_REQUESTS 10028 TRADE_RETCODE_LOCKED 10029 TRADE_RETCODE_FROZEN 10031 TRADE_RETCODE_CONNECTION (no connection)

docs.title: Validation — fix the request
docs.text: Code Name Common cause 10013 TRADE_RETCODE_INVALID malformed request 10014 TRADE_RETCODE_INVALID_VOLUME volume < min or > max / wrong step 10015 TRADE_RETCODE_INVALID_PRICE price breaks symbol rules 10016 TRADE_RETCODE_INVALID_STOPS SL/TP too close (StopLevel) 10022 TRADE_RETCODE_INVALID_EXPIRATION bad expiration time 10030 TRADE_RETCODE_INVALID_FILL fill type not allowed 10035 TRADE_RETCODE_INVALID_ORDER order type prohibited for symbol 10038 TRADE_RETCODE_INVALID_CLOSE_VOLUME close volume exceeds position

docs.title: Restrictions — check trading conditions
docs.text: Code Name 10017 TRADE_RETCODE_TRADE_DISABLED 10018 TRADE_RETCODE_MARKET_CLOSED 10026 TRADE_RETCODE_SERVER_DISABLES_AT 10027 TRADE_RETCODE_CLIENT_DISABLES_AT 10032 TRADE_RETCODE_ONLY_REAL 10042 TRADE_RETCODE_LONG_ONLY 10043 TRADE_RETCODE_SHORT_ONLY 10044 TRADE_RETCODE_CLOSE_ONLY 10045 TRADE_RETCODE_FIFO_CLOSE 10046 TRADE_RETCODE_HEDGE_PROHIBITED

docs.title: Limits — reduce volume / positions
docs.text: Code Name 10019 TRADE_RETCODE_NO_MONEY 10033 TRADE_RETCODE_LIMIT_ORDERS 10034 TRADE_RETCODE_LIMIT_VOLUME 10040 TRADE_RETCODE_LIMIT_POSITIONS

docs.title: State
docs.text: Code Name Meaning 10023 TRADE_RETCODE_ORDER_CHANGED order changed during the request 10025 TRADE_RETCODE_NO_CHANGES new params equal current — nothing to do 10036 TRADE_RETCODE_POSITION_CLOSED position already closed 10039 TRADE_RETCODE_CLOSE_ORDER_EXIST a close order already exists

docs.title: Rejection / processing
docs.text: Code Name 10006 TRADE_RETCODE_REJECT 10007 TRADE_RETCODE_CANCEL 10011 TRADE_RETCODE_ERROR 10041 TRADE_RETCODE_REJECT_CANCEL

docs.title: 🔁 A retry pattern
docs.text:
Categorise by RetCode and let trade_outcome_unknown? gate the uncertain ones:

REQUOTE   = [10_004, 10_020].freeze
TEMPORARY = [10_012, 10_021, 10_024, 10_028, 10_029, 10_031].freeze

def buy_with_retry(mt5, symbol, volume, tries: 3)
  tries.times do |i|
    r = mt5.buy_market(symbol, volume)
    return r if r.returned_code == 10_009
    code = r.returned_code
    break unless REQUOTE.include?(code) || TEMPORARY.include?(code)   # permanent → stop
    sleep(REQUOTE.include?(code) ? 0.1 : i + 1)                        # requote fast, temp backoff
  end
  nil
rescue MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError => e
  raise if e.trade_outcome_unknown?    # never auto-retry an uncertain trade
  raise
end

docs.title: 📑 Quick category reference
docs.text: Category RetCodes Action Success 10008, 10009, 10010 continue Requote 10004, 10020 retry immediately with a fresh price Temporary 10012, 10021, 10024, 10028, 10029, 10031 retry with a delay Validation 10013–10016, 10022, 10030, 10035, 10038 fix the request Restrictions 10017, 10018, 10026, 10027, 10032, 10042–10046 check conditions Limits 10019, 10033, 10034, 10040 reduce volume / positions State 10023, 10025, 10036, 10039 re-read current state Rejection 10006, 10007, 10011, 10041 inspect the request

docs.title: The MetaRPC SDK family
docs.text:
Where RubyMT5 sits — and how it pairs with the Trade Copier to mirror a strategy across accounts.

MetaRPC ships two families of SDKs. They share the same authentication (an ApiKey sent as gRPC metadata plus an owner user_key in the body), the same gRPC-over-TLS transport to *.mrpc.pro, the same mrpc.pro portal and the same demo onboarding — but they do different jobs.

Family Job Endpoint SDKs Terminal SDKs operate one trading account — connect, read, trade, stream mt5.mrpc.pro:443 (MT5) RubyMT5, GoMT5, CSharpMT5, CppMT5, NodeMT5, PyMT5 (+ MT4 variants) Copier SDKs mirror trades between accounts (master → followers) copy.mrpc.pro:443 RubyCopier, NodeCopier, GoCopier, CSharpCopier, PyCopier, …

RubyMT5 is a Terminal SDK. When you want to replicate what happens on one account to others, reach for the Copier SDK — in Ruby that's RubyCopier (metarpc_copier).

docs.title: How RubyMT5 and RubyCopier relate
docs.text:
RubyMT5 (this SDK) RubyCopier Scope one account a master → follower pair Does connect, quotes, buy_market, streams start · list · pause · remove a copier Endpoint mt5.mrpc.pro:443 copy.mrpc.pro:443 Thinks in ticks, orders, positions risk sizing, pause/resume, copy logs

One sentence: RubyMT5 is where trades are produced and observed on an account; RubyCopier is how they're distributed to followers.

docs.title: The bridge — a shared terminal session
docs.text:
A copier account carries an optional id — a terminal session GUID. That's exactly the value RubyMT5 obtains on connect: after connect / connect_ex, the session GUID (terminal_instance_guid) lives on mt5.account.server_guid. So an account you're already running with RubyMT5 can be enrolled into a copier without the copier reconnecting it — pass that GUID (hyphenated via RubyCopier.to_hyphen_guid) as the account id.

RubyCopier also understands MT5 account type values MT5 and MT5_MRPC (plus MT4, cTrader CT, TradeLocker TL) — the same MRPC-hosted terminals RubyMT5 drives.

docs.title: End-to-end: run a strategy on the master, replicate to a follower
docs.text:
require "metarpc_mt5"
require "rubycopier"      # git clone'd alongside; see Install below

KEY = ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"]   # owner key — note: TRIAL is NOT accepted by the copier

# 1 · Operate the MASTER account with RubyMT5
master = MetaRPC::MT5::MT5Sugar.create("mt5.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: KEY)
master.quick_connect(ENV["MASTER_LOGIN"].to_i, ENV["MASTER_PASSWORD"], "MetaQuotes-Demo")
master_session_id = RubyCopier.to_hyphen_guid(master.account.server_guid)  # the ConnectEx GUID → copier id

# 2 · Start a copier: MASTER → FOLLOWER (RubyCopier, on copy.mrpc.pro)
copier = RubyCopier::CopierService.new("copy.mrpc.pro:443", user_key: KEY)
rep = copier.start(
  risk_type:  "LotMultiplier",   # or "FixedLot" + risk_value "0.1"
  risk_value: "1.0",
  copy_sl: true, copy_tp: true,
  master: { type: "MT5", user: ENV["MASTER_LOGIN"].to_i, password: ENV["MASTER_PASSWORD"],
            server: "MetaQuotes-Demo", id: master_session_id },
  slave:  { type: "MT5", user: ENV["SLAVE_LOGIN"].to_i,  password: ENV["SLAVE_PASSWORD"],
            server: "MetaQuotes-Demo" },
)
abort "copier start failed: #{rep.error}" unless rep.ok
puts "copier ##{rep.copier_id} running"

# 3 · Trades you now place on the master via RubyMT5 replicate to the follower
master.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)
# … the copier mirrors the open (and the later close) onto the follower account

# 4 · Tidy up
copier.remove(rep.copier_id)

Install: RubyCopier isn't on RubyGems — clone it (git clone https://github.com/MetaRPC/RubyCopier.git && cd RubyCopier && bundle install) and require its lib/rubycopier, or point a Gemfile at the repo: gem "metarpc_copier", git: "https://github.com/MetaRPC/RubyCopier.git".

Risk sizing (the copier's risk_type): FixedLot · LotMultiplier · BalanceMultiplier · FixedBalanceMultiplier · EquityMultiplier. Plus copy_sl / copy_tp / copy_pending_orders / reverse_copy. Manage a running copier with copier.list, copier.pause(id, paused: true) and copier.remove(id).

docs.title: 🧩 Notes & gotchas
docs.text:
• Two services, two endpoints. RubyMT5 talks to mt5.mrpc.pro; RubyCopier to copy.mrpc.pro. The copier is a companion service, not a replacement.
  • Owner key required for the copier. TRIAL works for a first look on a terminal, but CopierService.new raises without a real owner user_key.
  • Transport success ≠ broker execution. A successful start means the copier was created — confirm the follower actually opened the trade (RubyCopier's logs, or read the follower with RubyMT5's open_positions).
  • Demo-first. Use disposable demo accounts for copier tests. Hosted terminals and running copiers are billed separately (see pricing).

docs.title: Synchronous Calls & Threaded Streaming
docs.text: How RubyMT5 actually executes: every request/response call is synchronous and blocking; the only concurrency is streaming on background threads. There is no async/await or Fiber API.

docs.title: 🎯 The model in one line
docs.text:
• Request/response calls (account info, quotes, trading, history) block the calling thread and return a value (or raise). Linear, simple, predictable.
  • Streaming calls (subscribe_ticks, on_trade, …) run on a background thread and invoke your block per message, returning a Subscription immediately — your main thread keeps going.
  • Want parallelism for blocking calls? Spawn your own Ruby Threads. The gRPC layer releases the GVL while waiting on the network, so independent calls can be in flight at once.
Blocking call Background-thread stream Returns the result value a Subscription (immediately) Blocks your thread? yes, until the reply no — the block runs on the reader thread Use for everything request/response live ticks, trade & P/L events Stop it n/a (it already returned) sub.cancel

docs.title: ✅ Synchronous calls (the default — everything)
docs.text:
Just call and use the result. No await, no runtime to set up:

require "metarpc_mt5"

mt5 = MetaRPC::MT5::MT5Sugar.create("mt5.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])
mt5.connect(5057947437, "password", server: "MetaQuotes-Demo")

a = mt5.account_info          # blocks, returns an Account Struct
q = mt5.price("EURUSD")       # blocks, returns a Quote
r = mt5.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)   # blocks, returns OrderSendData
puts "balance #{a.balance}  bid #{q.bid}  trade #{r.returned_code}"

This is the right model for CLI scripts, one-off tasks, notebooks, and the demos — read top to bottom.

docs.title: 🧵 Concurrency with your own threads
docs.text:
Because each call blocks only its own thread, you parallelise by spawning threads. Independent reads then wait concurrently instead of one-after-another:

# Quote several symbols at once
symbols = %w[EURUSD GBPUSD USDJPY XAUUSD]
quotes  = symbols.map { |s| Thread.new { [s, mt5.price(s)] } }.map(&:value).to_h
quotes.each { |s, q| puts "#{s}  #{q.bid} / #{q.ask}" }

Share carefully. One connected mt5 multiplexes fine for reads over gRPC. For heavy concurrent trading, prefer a separate connection per worker (pass a stable id: per strategy) so sessions don't interleave. Guard any shared mutable state you build yourself with a Mutex.

docs.title: 📡 Streaming is the built-in concurrency
docs.text:
A streaming method hands the work to a background thread and returns a Subscription. Your main thread is free while the block runs per message:

sub = mt5.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") { |t| puts "#{t.bid} / #{t.ask}" }
# ... main thread keeps working ...
sleep 5
sub.cancel          # stop cleanly (joins the reader thread)

Need a blocking sample instead? each_tick runs the stream inline for a fixed time and returns the count:

n = mt5.each_tick("EURUSD", seconds: 5) { |t| puts t.bid }

Full lifecycle, patterns and pitfalls (including don't cancel from inside the block): gRPC Stream Management.

docs.title: 💡 Rules of thumb
docs.text:
1. Default to straight synchronous code. It's the whole request/response API and it's the simplest thing that works.
  2. Use streaming for live data — it's already concurrent (a background thread), so you don't manage threads yourself.
  3. Add threads only when you have independent blocking work (e.g. many symbols) and the wall-clock saving matters.
  4. Background jobs (a cron task, a Sidekiq/Resque worker) run this synchronous code as-is — nothing special required.
  5. There is no async/await here. If you see await or connect_by_server_name in an example, it's from another language's SDK — the Ruby API is MT5Sugar.create(...) + connect.

docs.text:

docs.title: Translating RubyMT5 docs
docs.text: The docs are internationalised with mkdocs-static-i18n (suffix structure). English is the source; 27 target languages are configured. This page is the skeleton for translators.

docs.title: How it works (the mechanism)
docs.text:
• Language switcher — the globe menu in the header lists every configured language; it's generated automatically from the plugin config in mkdocs.yml.
  • Fallback — a page with no translation falls back to English, so every language already works end-to-end. You translate pages one at a time; nothing breaks in the meantime.
  • URLs — English is at the root (/RubyMT5/…), each language under its locale (/RubyMT5/zh/…, /RubyMT5/ja/…, …).

You don't pre-create blank files for every page — that would hide the English fallback behind empty pages. Create a translation file only when you actually translate that page.

docs.title: How to translate a page
docs.text:
Suffix structure: put the translation next to the English file, with the locale before .md.

docs/All_Guides/GETTING_STARTED.md        # English (source)
docs/All_Guides/GETTING_STARTED.zh.md     # 简体中文
docs/All_Guides/GETTING_STARTED.ja.md     # 日本語
docs/index.md                             # English home
docs/index.ja.md                          # 日本語 home

Steps:

  1. Copy the English page.md to page.<locale>.md.
  2. Translate the prose. Keep unchanged: code blocks, Ruby/API names, enum constants (:SYMBOL_DIGITS, TMT5_ORDER_TYPE_BUY), file paths, links, and front-matter keys (hide:, description:).
  3. Build (python -m mkdocs build) or serve (python -m mkdocs serve) and check the page under /<locale>/.

Translate in this order (highest value first): index → All_Guides/GETTING_STARTED → MT5_For_Beginners → Your_First_Project → GLOSSARY → RETURN_CODES_REFERENCE, then the rest. The deep API/method pages (MT5Account / MT5Service / MT5Sugar) are read mostly in English and can come last.

docs.title: Right-to-left languages
docs.text: ar, fa, ur, he are right-to-left — with reconfigure_material: true the Material theme flips the layout automatically for those locales. Keep code/paths LTR (Markdown handles this).

docs.title: UserCode Sandbox
docs.text: Your blank canvas inside the demo suite — sugar arrives already connected, so you write only the trading logic.

docs.title: 🏁 Quick start
docs.text:
1. Open examples/demos/usercode/18_usercode.rb.
  2. Write your code inside the registered block (below the write your code below marker).
  3. Run it:
ruby examples/demos/main.rb 18

That's it — the menu connects once, then hands your block a live, connected sugar.

The sandbox as it ships:

Demos.register("18", "Sandbox - your own code (edit 18_usercode.rb)") do |sugar, cfg|
  sym = cfg.test_symbol

  # ─── write your code below ───
  puts "  balance #{format('%.2f', sugar.balance)}   #{sym} bid #{sugar.bid(sym)}"

  #   q    = sugar.service.quote(sym)
  #   tick = sugar.account.symbol_info_tick(sym)
  #   sugar.buy_market(sym, cfg.test_volume)   # ⚠ trades on a demo account
end

Keep it read-only while experimenting, or use tiny volumes on a demo account.

docs.title: 🎁 What's already set up
docs.text:
The block receives two arguments:

Argument What it is sugar a connected MT5Sugar — the high-level one-liners cfg the loaded config: cfg.test_symbol, cfg.test_volume, cfg.user, cfg.server, …

And from sugar you can reach every layer:

sugar            # MT5Sugar  — one-liners
sugar.service    # MT5Service — typed Structs (Quote, Account)
sugar.account    # MT5Account — raw gRPC / protobuf

No connect call, no API key handling — the launcher did it. Config comes from examples/demos/config/config.json or the MT5_LOGIN / MT5_PASSWORD / MT5_SERVER / MT5_SYMBOL / MT5_VOLUME env vars.

docs.title: 🧩 Mixing the three layers
docs.text:
All three are live at once — drop down whenever the sugar layer doesn't expose what you need:

# High — MT5Sugar
bal = sugar.balance                       # => Float

# Mid — MT5Service (typed Struct)
q = sugar.service.quote("EURUSD")         # Quote(bid, ask, spread, …)

# Low — MT5Account (raw protobuf)
tick = sugar.account.symbol_info_tick("EURUSD")   # raw MrpcMqlTick

docs.title: 📘 Quick reference (MT5Sugar)
docs.text:
# ── Account ──────────────────────────────────────────────
sugar.balance            # Float
sugar.equity             # balance + floating P/L
sugar.free_margin        # available to open more
sugar.margin_level       # %
sugar.account_info       # Struct(login, balance, currency, leverage, …)
sugar.demo?              # true on a demo account

# ── Prices ───────────────────────────────────────────────
sugar.bid("EURUSD")      # Float
sugar.ask("EURUSD")
sugar.spread("EURUSD")
sugar.price("EURUSD")    # Quote(bid, ask, spread, …)

# ── Market orders (return OrderSendData — check returned_code) ──
r = sugar.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)
r = sugar.sell_market("EURUSD", 0.01)
r = sugar.buy_market_with_sl_tp("EURUSD", 0.01, sl: 1.0820, tp: 1.0920)

# ── Pending orders ───────────────────────────────────────
sugar.buy_limit("EURUSD", 0.01, 1.0850)
sugar.sell_stop("EURUSD", 0.01, 1.0750)

# ── Positions ────────────────────────────────────────────
sugar.open_positions(symbol: "EURUSD")   # Array
sugar.count_positions
sugar.total_profit
sugar.has_position?("EURUSD")
sugar.close_position(ticket)
sugar.close_all_positions
sugar.close_all_by_symbol("EURUSD")
sugar.modify_sl_tp(ticket, stop_loss: 1.0830, take_profit: 1.0930)

# ── History (needs from_utc:) ────────────────────────────
sugar.order_history(from_utc: Time.now.utc - 24 * 3600)
sugar.positions_history(from_utc: Time.now.utc - 7 * 86_400)

# ── Symbols & risk sizing ────────────────────────────────
sugar.symbol_digits("EURUSD")
sugar.symbol_point("EURUSD")
sugar.min_stop_level("EURUSD")
sugar.required_margin("EURUSD", 0.10, sugar.ask("EURUSD"))
sugar.calc_profit("EURUSD", 0.10, 1.0900, 1.0950)        # type: :buy by default
sugar.max_lot("EURUSD", sugar.ask("EURUSD"))

# ── Streaming (block + Subscription) ─────────────────────
sub = sugar.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") { |t| puts t.bid }   # sub.cancel to stop
n   = sugar.each_tick("EURUSD", seconds: 5) { |t| puts t.bid }  # blocking

Full lists: MT5Sugar · MT5Service · MT5Account.

docs.title: ✅ Checking a trade
docs.text:
Trade one-liners return the result data — they don't raise on a broker rejection. Check returned_code (10009 = done); a hard failure raises MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError:

begin
  r = sugar.buy_market(sym, cfg.test_volume)
  if r.returned_code == 10_009
    puts "opened ##{r.order} @ #{r.price}"
  else
    puts "rejected: #{r.returned_string_code} — #{r.returned_code_description}"
  end
rescue MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError => e
  raise if e.trade_outcome_unknown?     # uncertain — check positions before retrying
  warn "trade error: #{e.error.mql_error_trade_description}"
end

See Return Codes & the error model for the full picture.

docs.title: 📝 A complete sandbox example
docs.text:
Risk-size a trade to ~1% of balance, open it, then report:

Demos.register("18", "Sandbox - your own code") do |sugar, cfg|
  sym = cfg.test_symbol
  q   = sugar.price(sym)
  pip = sugar.symbol_point(sym) * 10
  dig = sugar.symbol_digits(sym)

  sl  = (q.bid - 20 * pip).round(dig)                      # 20-pip stop
  tp  = (q.ask + 40 * pip).round(dig)

  loss_at_01 = -sugar.calc_profit(sym, 0.1, q.ask, sl)     # loss on 0.1 lot if stopped
  lots = [(0.1 * (sugar.balance * 0.01) / loss_at_01).round(2), 0.01].max

  if sugar.required_margin(sym, lots, q.ask) > sugar.free_margin
    puts "  not enough free margin for #{lots} lots"
  else
    r = sugar.buy_market_with_sl_tp(sym, lots, sl: sl, tp: tp)
    puts r.returned_code == 10_009 ? "  opened ##{r.order} (#{lots} lots)" : "  #{r.returned_code_description}"
  end

  puts "  open: #{sugar.count_positions}  floating P/L: #{sugar.total_profit.round(2)}"
end

docs.title: 💡 Tips & common mistakes
docs.text:
1. Start read-only. sugar.balance, sugar.price(sym), sugar.open_positions can't hurt anything — learn the shapes first.
  2. Trade on demo, tiny volumes. Use cfg.test_volume (0.01) and confirm sugar.demo? before trading.
  3. Check returned_code. A returned result is not proof of success — 10009 is. Catching exceptions alone is not enough.
  4. Don't re-raise an uncertain trade blindly. On trade_outcome_unknown?, check open_positions first — the SDK never auto-resends a trade.
  5. Enum values are symbols (:ACCOUNT_BALANCE), not constants — see ENUMs Reference.
  6. Unsure of a field or enum name? Ask the Protobuf Inspector.

docs.title: Your First Project
docs.text: Build a small, complete RubyMT5 script: connect, quote, trade with risk sizing, and report.

docs.title: 1 · Set up
docs.text:
mkdir mt5-bot && cd mt5-bot

Point Bundler at the repo (the gem isn't on RubyGems), then install:

# Gemfile
source "https://rubygems.org"
gem "metarpc_mt5", git: "https://github.com/MetaRPC/RubyMT5.git"
gem "grpc", "~> 1.84.1" if Gem.win_platform?   # Windows: prebuilt binary

bundle install

Create bot.rb. (Prefer the ready-made examples? git clone the repo and read examples/demos/ — see Getting Started.)

docs.title: 2 · Connect
docs.text:
require "metarpc_mt5"

mt5 = MetaRPC::MT5::MT5Sugar.create("mt5.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])
mt5.quick_connect(
  ENV["MT5_LOGIN"].to_i,
  ENV["MT5_PASSWORD"],
  ENV["MT5_SERVER"],          # e.g. MetaQuotes-Demo
)
puts "connected? #{mt5.connected?}"

Need the MRPC_API_KEY? Register at https://mrpc.pro/signup — your key is provisioned automatically and shown in the MT5 Client API Explorer (Copy key). See Getting Started → API Key. (Or pass "TRIAL" for keyless access while testing.)

docs.title: 3 · Look at the market
docs.text:
symbol = "EURUSD"
q = mt5.price(symbol)
pips = (q.spread / mt5.symbol_point(symbol) / 10).round(1)
puts "#{symbol}  bid #{q.bid}  ask #{q.ask}  #{pips} pips"

docs.title: 4 · Trade with risk sizing
docs.text:
digits = mt5.symbol_digits(symbol)
pip    = mt5.symbol_point(symbol) * 10          # 1 pip on a 5-digit symbol
sl     = (q.bid - 20 * pip).round(digits)       # 20-pip stop
tp     = (q.ask + 40 * pip).round(digits)       # 40-pip target

# Size so the 20-pip stop risks ~1% of balance:
loss_per_01 = -mt5.calc_profit(symbol, 0.1, q.ask, sl)        # loss on 0.1 lot if stopped
lots = [(0.1 * (mt5.balance * 0.01) / loss_per_01).round(2), 0.01].max

# Can we afford the margin?
if mt5.required_margin(symbol, lots, q.ask) > mt5.free_margin
  abort "not enough free margin for #{lots} lots"
end

r = mt5.buy_market_with_sl_tp(symbol, lots, sl: sl, tp: tp, comment: "first-project")
puts r.returned_code == 10_009 ? "opened ##{r.order} with #{lots} lots" : r.returned_code_description

docs.title: 5 · Manage & report
docs.text:
puts "open positions: #{mt5.count_positions}"
puts "floating P/L: #{mt5.total_profit.round(2)}"

# tidy up for the demo
mt5.close_all_positions

# today's realized result
from = Time.now.utc - 24 * 3600
deals = mt5.order_history(from_utc: from).filter_map { |h| h.history_deal }
puts "today: #{deals.size} deals, net #{deals.sum(&:profit).round(2)}"

docs.text:
MT5_LOGIN=5057947437 MT5_PASSWORD=secret MT5_SERVER=MetaQuotes-Demo \
MRPC_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY bundle exec ruby bot.rb

docs.title: MT5Account — Master Overview
docs.text:
One page to orient fast: what lives where, how to choose the right API, and jump links to every overview and method spec in this docs set.

MetaRPC::MT5::MT5Account (from the metarpc_mt5 gem) is the low-level layer — a thin, 1:1-with-the-wire client. Each method maps to a single gRPC RPC: you pass the plain arguments, it builds the generated protobuf *Request, sends it with the APIKey + terminal-id metadata, and returns the reply's *Data payload — or raises MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError. It owns the gRPC channel, the service stubs, the auth metadata and the connection lifecycle.

require "metarpc_mt5"
acct = MetaRPC::MT5::MT5Account.new("mt5.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])

When to use this layer

Use MT5Account when you need a field the friendly layers do not expose, or full control over the exact request. For everyday work prefer MT5Service (plain args + typed Structs) or MT5Sugar (one-liners).

docs.title: 🔌 Usage pattern (raw gRPC)
docs.text:
Every method is called on an MT5Account. It owns the gRPC channel, sends the terminal id and API key as metadata, and unwraps the reply — returning the protobuf *Data payload or raising an error.

require "metarpc_mt5"

# Create the client (prepares the gRPC channel; api_key from MRPC_API_KEY)
acct = MetaRPC::MT5::MT5Account.new("mt5.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])

# Connect the terminal (ConnectEx by broker server name).
# The gateway returns a terminal session GUID; later calls reuse it automatically.
acct.connect(5057947437, "password", server: "MetaQuotes-Demo")

# Call a method: returns the *Data payload, or raises ApiError / a gRPC error.
s = acct.account_summary
puts "Balance: #{s.account_balance} #{s.account_currency}"

Every method follows the same shape:

  • Proto Service/Method: Service.Method(Request) → Reply
  • Client call: acct.method(args) returns the *Data payload.
  • Reply structure: the reply carries either a data payload or an error; MT5Account returns the data and turns error into a raised ApiError.
  • Errors are exceptions — there are no error return values; wrap calls in begin/rescue.

Field access: the generated protobuf messages expose snake_case readers — s.account_balance, not getAccountBalance(). The friendly MT5Service layer converts these into plain Ruby Structs for you.

Timestamps: proto uses google.protobuf.Timestamp (or raw unix seconds on some messages); read .seconds. MT5Service returns numbers / UTC instead.

Streaming methods: return a Subscription handle. The SDK reads the stream on a background thread and invokes your block for each payload; call subscription.cancel to stop.

docs.title: Layer 1: MT5Account (Low-Level) — You are here!
docs.text: What: direct protobuf/gRPC communication with the MT5 terminal. Plain arguments in, protobuf *Data out; complete access to every MT5 function; highest control. Location: lib/metarpc_mt5/mt5_account.rb.

docs.title: Layer 2: MT5Service
docs.text: What: a friendly facade over MT5Account — plain arguments and typed Ruby Structs (Account, Quote…). No protobuf. Location: lib/metarpc_mt5/mt5_service.rb → overview.

docs.title: Layer 3: MT5Sugar
docs.text:
What: high-level convenience API — one-liners, risk-based position sizing, smart defaults. Location: lib/metarpc_mt5/mt5_sugar.rb → overview.

Each layer owns the one below it: MT5Sugar owns an MT5Service, which owns an MT5Account. From Sugar you can always reach down with sugar.service and sugar.account. (MetaRPC::MT5::Client aliases MT5Sugar; MetaRPC::MT5::Account aliases MT5Account.)

docs.title: 💡 Key concepts
docs.text:
• Errors are exceptions. A server-side rejection raises MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError (carrying the mql / trade codes); a transport failure raises the gRPC error. There are no error return values.
  • Session id is automatic. connect (ConnectEx) obtains a terminal session GUID; the SDK attaches it (+ your api key) to every later call and stream. Pass a stable id: per strategy so the gateway reuses one terminal.
  • Trade retcode. order_send / order_close carry a trade-server result code — 10009 = DONE (success). See Return Codes.
  • MT5 has positions. Unlike MT4, MT5 separates positions (net market exposure), orders (pending/working) and deals (executed transactions in history).

"Trade safe, code clean, and may your gRPC streams always flow smoothly."

docs.title: 🔢 Reading One Double Account Property
docs.text:
Request: a single floating-point account property (AccountInfoDoubleData) — balance, equity, margin, profit, credit and more — selected by an enum.

API Information:

  • Low-level API: MT5Account#account_info_double(property) (from the metarpc_mt5 gem)
  • gRPC service: mt5_term_api.AccountInformation
  • Proto definition: AccountInfoDouble (defined in mt5-term-api-account-information.proto)

docs.title: RPC
docs.text:
• Service: mt5_term_api.AccountInformation
  • Method: AccountInfoDouble(AccountInfoDoubleRequest) → AccountInfoDoubleReply
  • Low-level client (generated): Mt5TermApi::AccountInformation::Stub#account_info_double(request, metadata:, deadline:)

docs.title: 💬 Just the essentials
docs.text:
• What it is. One RPC that returns a single Float account metric, chosen by a property enum.
  • Why you need it. Lighter than the full account_summary when you only need one number — e.g. free margin before sizing a trade.
  • Sanity check. account_info_double(:ACCOUNT_BALANCE) matches account_summary.account_balance.

docs.title: 🎯 Purpose
docs.text: Read one double property on demand. The money-management essentials live here — :ACCOUNT_MARGIN_FREE (can I afford this trade?), :ACCOUNT_PROFIT (floating P/L), :ACCOUNT_MARGIN_LEVEL (margin health). For several values at once, call account_summary once instead of many single reads.

docs.title: 🧱 Signature
docs.text:
class MetaRPC::MT5::MT5Account
  # Returns one ACCOUNT_* double property. `property` is an
  # AccountInfoDoublePropertyType symbol (e.g. :ACCOUNT_EQUITY).
  def account_info_double(property) -> Float
end

Request message: AccountInfoDoubleRequest { AccountInfoDoublePropertyType property_id = 1; } Reply: the SDK returns data.requested_value (a Float).

docs.title: 🔽 Input
docs.text: Parameter Type Description property Symbol (AccountInfoDoublePropertyType) Which double property to read. Required.

docs.title: ⬆️ Output
docs.text: A single Float — the requested property's value.

docs.title: 🧱 Property enum — AccountInfoDoublePropertyType
docs.text:
enum AccountInfoDoublePropertyType {
  ACCOUNT_BALANCE            = 0;   // account balance (deposit currency)
  ACCOUNT_CREDIT             = 1;   // credit
  ACCOUNT_PROFIT             = 2;   // current floating profit
  ACCOUNT_EQUITY             = 3;   // equity = balance + floating P/L
  ACCOUNT_MARGIN             = 4;   // margin used by open positions
  ACCOUNT_MARGIN_FREE        = 5;   // free margin for new positions
  ACCOUNT_MARGIN_LEVEL       = 6;   // margin level, percent
  ACCOUNT_MARGIN_SO_CALL     = 7;   // margin call level
  ACCOUNT_MARGIN_SO_SO       = 8;   // stop-out level
  ACCOUNT_MARGIN_INITIAL     = 9;   // reserved initial margin
  ACCOUNT_MARGIN_MAINTENANCE = 10;  // reserved maintenance margin
  ACCOUNT_ASSETS             = 11;  // current assets
  ACCOUNT_LIABILITIES        = 12;  // current liabilities
  ACCOUNT_COMMISSION_BLOCKED = 13;  // blocked commission
}

docs.title: 🧩 Notes & Tips
docs.text:
• Errors are exceptions: raises MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError on a server rejection; wrap in begin/rescue.
  • Pass the symbol, not the number — :ACCOUNT_EQUITY, not 3.
  • The full snapshot is cheaper for many values — if you need several, call account_summary once.
  • Floating profit is :ACCOUNT_PROFIT here, or account_equity - account_balance from the summary.

docs.title: 1) Free margin before trading
docs.text:
free = acct.account_info_double(:ACCOUNT_MARGIN_FREE)
puts "free margin: #{free.round(2)}"

docs.title: 2) Floating profit
docs.text:
profit = acct.account_info_double(:ACCOUNT_PROFIT)
puts profit.positive? ? "In profit: +#{profit.round(2)}" : "Down: #{profit.round(2)}"

docs.title: 3) Margin-health gauge
docs.text:
level = acct.account_info_double(:ACCOUNT_MARGIN_LEVEL)
puts case
     when level.zero?   then "No open margin"
     when level < 100   then "⚠️ Critical"
     when level < 200   then "⚠️ Low"
     else                    "✅ Healthy"
     end

docs.title: 4) Equity vs balance (floating)
docs.text:
eq  = acct.account_info_double(:ACCOUNT_EQUITY)
bal = acct.account_info_double(:ACCOUNT_BALANCE)
puts "floating: #{(eq - bal).round(2)}"

docs.title: Affordability check
docs.text:
def can_afford?(acct, margin_needed)
  acct.account_info_double(:ACCOUNT_MARGIN_FREE) >= margin_needed
rescue MetaRPC::MT5::ApiError
  false
end

  • AccountInfoInteger · AccountInfoString — integer / string properties.
  • Friendly layer: MT5Sugar#balance / #equity / #margin / #free_margin · MT5Service#account_info_double.

docs.title: 🧱 Property enum — AccountInfoIntegerPropertyType
docs.text:
enum AccountInfoIntegerPropertyType {
  ACCOUNT_LOGIN           = 0;   // account login (ID)
  ACCOUNT_TRADE_MODE      = 1;   // 0 demo · 1 contest · 2 real
  ACCOUNT_LEVERAGE        = 2;   // leverage (e.g. 100)
  ACCOUNT_LIMIT_ORDERS    = 3;   // max active pending orders
  ACCOUNT_MARGIN_SO_MODE  = 4;   // stop-out mode (percent / money)
  ACCOUNT_TRADE_ALLOWED   = 5;   // trading allowed (0/1)
  ACCOUNT_TRADE_EXPERT    = 6;   // EA trading allowed (0/1)
  ACCOUNT_MARGIN_MODE     = 7;   // 0 netting · 1 exchange · 2 hedging
  ACCOUNT_CURRENCY_DIGITS = 8;   // currency decimal places
  ACCOUNT_FIFO_CLOSE      = 9;   // FIFO close required (0/1)
  ACCOUNT_HEDGE_ALLOWED   = 10;  // hedging allowed (0/1)
}

docs.title: 🧩 Notes & Tips
docs.text:
• Errors are exceptions: raises ApiError; wrap in begin/rescue.
  • Boolean-ish flags come back as 0/1 — compare == 1 or use .positive?.
  • Leverage drives margin requirements — read it once and cache it per session.
  • :ACCOUNT_TRADE_MODE returns 0/1/2 as a plain Integer here (the typed symbol is on account_summary).

docs.title: 1) Leverage & login
docs.text: puts "Login #{acct.account_info_integer(:ACCOUNT_LOGIN)}  leverage 1:#{acct.account_info_integer(:ACCOUNT_LEVERAGE)}"

docs.title: 2) Is automated trading allowed?

ea_ok = acct.account_info_integer(:ACCOUNT_TRADE_EXPERT) == 1
puts ea_ok ? "EAs allowed" : "EA trading disabled"

docs.title: 3) Margin mode

mode = acct.account_info_integer(:ACCOUNT_MARGIN_MODE)
puts ["netting", "exchange", "hedging"][mode] || "unknown"

docs.title: 4) Trade permission gate
docs.text:
unless acct.account_info_integer(:ACCOUNT_TRADE_ALLOWED) == 1
  abort "trading is disabled for this account"
end

docs.title: Cache identity & leverage once

def account_facts(acct)
  {
    login: acct.account_info_integer(:ACCOUNT_LOGIN),
    leverage: acct.account_info_integer(:ACCOUNT_LEVERAGE),
    ea_allowed: acct.account_info_integer(:ACCOUNT_TRADE_EXPERT) == 1,
  }
end
